newsitem.title: SPAIN: Basque parties fail to unite against violence.
newsitem.headline: Basque parties fail to unite against violence.

text.p: Political parties in Spain's Basque region failed on Friday to agree a common strategy to fight resurgent separatist violence, dashing hopes for a breakthrough in the long-running conflict with ETA rebels.

A meeting of the parties in Vitoria, the seat of the Basque regional government, had been expected to last into the night. But it ended abruptly after about three hours with no communique on a unified plan to fight escalating attacks.

The parties reaffirmed Basque President Jose Antonio Ardanza's offer, first made last June, to open a dialogue with the violent Basque separatist group ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) if it ceases violence and releases two hostages.

But officials said they could not overcome fundamental differences on how to respond to growing street violence by Basque youths, on where ETA prisoners should serve their terms and on how to bring about negotiations to end the conflict.
"If at this moment we are stuck because of different views, we consider the future open," said Xabier Arzalluz, president of the Basque Nationalist Party (PNV) which heads the regional government.
The six parties were meeting as the Ajuria Enea pact, a forum set up in 1988 to seek the "pacification and normalisation" of the turbulent Basque region in the north.

The pact groups Basque branches of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's Popular Party and the opposition Socialists with nationalist parties. Herri Batasuna, the political arm of ETA, is the only parliamentary party not in the pact.
The Ajuria Enea intended to show a unified stance against violence after four deadly attacks by separatists in the past two weeks.
The meeting had raised hopes for a breakthrough on both sides of the conflict.
But beyond reaffirming the offer of dialogue, the parties agreed only that they would meet again every three months to continue looking for ways to bridge the gaps.
Politicians had said before the meeting that divisions between the nationalists on the one hand and the PP and Socialists on the other creates fertile ground for violence.
"ETA would last 10 minutes if the parties advance in Ajuria Enea," Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja said recently.
Even within the nationalist camp, there are deep rifts on whether to press for negotiations with ETA now that it has stepped up attacks.

The Ajuria Enea pact had been rendered ineffective in recent years when the nationalists pursued a more conciliatory stance towards Herri Batasuna. Meanwhile, the Popular Party was taking a firm line on ETA to draw voters in its 1996 election campaign.
The nationalists and the PP are also divided over where more than 500 ETA prisoners should serve out their terms.
The Basque parliament approved an appeal on Thursday to transfer of all Basque prisoners, including ETA members, to jails within 300 km (200 miles) of the Basque country.

The former Socialist government had adopted a "dispersion" policy which spread ETA prisoners all over the country in small groups and Aznar's administration rejects any blanket relocation. But it has agreed to consider moves on a case-by-case basis.

The PP and Socialists rejected the initiative, which also proposed sending a parliamentary delegation to present the idea to a minister in Madrid and to the jailed leader of ETA prisoners Juan Lorenza Lasa Mitxelena.
"It is an error to open a process of dialogue with an ETA interlocutor," Deputy Prime Minister Alvarez Cascos said of the plan.
